mappings.note: Why an ammeter must be low-resistance if the circuit current is to be read faithfully - meter behaviour, the second half of LO-5. The resistance here is the instrument's, not a conductor's, so no C 2.4 outcome is graded.
Asks for H = VIt, the statement of Joule heating. Kept with LO-2 rather than C 2.5-LO-1 because the quantity produced is heat in a conductor, not the power rating or energy bill of an appliance.

Who the ohm is named after. Poor fit like the parallel 'ampere' item: the graded answer is a name, not a relation, so LO-1 would be a pretence. Cited at competency level and reported as trivia with no outcome.

Material choice for a lamp filament: LO-2 owns the filament lamp, LO-3 owns the resistivity/material judgement behind the choice. Note the stored answer says tungsten has 'low resistivity', which contradicts the usual justification and looks like an answer-key error.
Operational meaning of 1 ohm as 1 volt producing 1 ampere - Ohm's law used to define the unit. Distinct from the resistivity-unit items, which belong to LO-3.
Energy = power x time, the relation LO-1 needs before any kWh calculation. Stating rather than substituting, but the same outcome as the billing items.
What a commercial 'unit' means - one kilowatt hour, priced. This is the kWh clause of LO-1 in its everyday-billing form; no heat is produced or dissipated, so C 2.5-LO-2 is the wrong sibling.
Conventional current direction versus electron flow. Not covered by any outcome - LO-1 uses current only as a magnitude in V = IR and says nothing about its direction. Content gap.
Sub-multiple of the ampere. Belongs with the current-unit gap; there is no outcome about units of current, unlike the ohm which LO-1 defines.

Builds the water-pipe analogy for potential difference driving current. Cited at C 8.1 because the graded skill is constructing a model of a phenomenon, and at C 2.4 for the potential-difference content; C 8.1-LO-5 is wrong since no circuit diagram or meter is involved.
SI unit of potential. Same uncovered ground as the other volt items; recorded under the potential-difference gap rather than stretched onto LO-1.

Numeric substitution into W = QV with a 10 V difference. The only numerical item in this part that never touches resistance or current, so no C 2.4 outcome fits - a clear instance of the missing potential-difference outcome.
Perfect conductor and perfect insulator defined by zero and infinite resistivity - the material clause of LO-3 taken to its limits.
Asks for R = rho*l/A, the expression that encodes all three LO-3 dependencies at once. Not LO-1: the expected answer is the geometric formula, not R = V/I.
Compares the resistivity of an alloy with that of its parent metal - a material comparison with geometry irrelevant, which is LO-3's core.
Why nichrome for a heater element. LO-2 leads because the heater is the named application; LO-3 is the material-property half (high resistivity, high melting point) that supplies the reason.

Three genuinely separate steps: define resistivity and use R = rho*l/A when l doubles (LO-3), then V = IR at fixed V to halve the current (LO-1), with the result read as an ammeter deflection (LO-5). One of the few items here where all three are graded rather than assumed.

Ranks pure metals by resistivity - LO-3 material clause. Flagged separately: the stored answer gives mercury at 94e-8 ohm m as the minimum, which is in fact the largest pure-metal value in the standard table (silver is the minimum), so the key looks wrong.

Same LO-3 ranking demand, for alloys. Also key-suspect: nichrome is quoted as the minimum-resistivity alloy when it is normally the highest, and the quoted 100e-6 ohm m does not match the usual table.
Highest-resistivity insulator. Same material-ranking family as the two items above; no geometry or circuit quantity involved.

Resistance rising with temperature. LO-3 is the nearest legal code but it enumerates only length, area of cross-section and material - temperature is named in no outcome, so this is a genuine coverage gap rather than a clean fit.
Alloy versus parent metal by resistivity, stated as a general rule rather than for a named pair - same outcome as the constantan/copper item, and they honestly share it.

Why alloys are used in heating devices. LO-2 for the heating-device application; LO-3 for the material argument. The reason given (oxidation resistance) is chemical durability, which no outcome covers, so LO-3 carries it only as 'material'.
Interprets a numerical resistivity value as the resistance of a unit cube of the material - this is LO-3's length-and-area dependence read backwards out of the constant.
Resistivity is unchanged when a wire is stretched. The whole item is the material-versus-geometry distinction of LO-3; answering with a changed R would be the intended error.
